title: Eggs — Physical, Chemical, Nutritional and Functional Characteristics
shortDescription: Structure, composition, grading and quality tests, and why eggs perform so many jobs in food.
genZNote: The egg is nature's multi-tool: foam, glue, emulsifier, gel. Yolk lecithin makes mayo; white proteins make meringue.

sections.heading: Physical Structure and Quality
bullets: Parts: shell (~94–95% CaCO3, cuticle, pores), shell membranes, albumen (thick and thin), yolk (vitelline membrane), chalazae, air cell.
Quality tests: candling (air-cell size, yolk shadow, blood spots), Haugh unit (albumen height vs weight), yolk index, specific gravity, floatation test.
On storage: air cell enlarges, albumen thins and pH rises from ~7.6 to ~9.2, so older eggs float more.

sections.heading: Chemical and Nutritional Composition
sections.body: Egg protein has the highest biological value among common foods; moderate intake is compatible with healthy diets, subject to individual lipid status.

table.caption: Egg composition
rows: Complete protein, B12, A, D, choline
Contains antimicrobial lysozyme; avidin binds biotin
~32% (triglycerides, phospholipids such as lecithin, cholesterol ~185–210 mg/egg)

sections.heading: Functional Properties
bullets: Foaming (albumen) for meringues and cakes; emulsifying (yolk lecithin) for mayonnaise; coagulation/gelation (white sets ~60–65 °C, yolk ~65–70 °C) for custards and binding; leavening; clarifying (consommé); colouring and glazing.
Safety: Salmonella in/on eggs; avoid raw egg dishes; pasteurised liquid egg; refrigerate; cook until firm.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Eggs are nutrient-dense foods whose structure and chemistry give them multifunctional roles in cooking and food manufacture.

highYieldFacts: Yolk has the lipids; albumen has the protein.
commonTraps: Do not say egg shells are mostly protein — mostly calcium carbonate.
